A lead-free profile
your boards actually repeat.

S-6600-PC is a 12-zone lead-free reflow oven with a 2300 mm heated tunnel, a 350 mm mesh conveyor and an industrial PC running PID closed-loop control to high-power SSR drivers. Six upper zones and six lower zones are driven independently, so the board can be warmed from underneath while the top surface is kept just hot enough to stop it warping. Control precision is quoted at ±1 °C and the controller scans every zone once a second.

01 — Why lead-free reflow is hard

Three ways a reflow oven costs you money without ever breaking down

A reflow oven rarely fails loudly. It drifts. A zone loses three degrees, a rail deforms a fraction of a millimetre, a chamber leaks nitrogen you are paying for by the cubic metre. None of that stops the line. All of it shows up in yield and in the utility bill.

Thermal inconsistency becomes yield loss

High-density boards and shielded components do not see the same temperature as the open pads beside them. On a lead-free profile running to 210–230 °C the gap shows up as cold joints on one part and thermal damage on another, and neither is visible until the AOI or the field return.

Energy and gas inefficiency drain the margin

Holding a tunnel at reflow temperature is a continuous power draw. A poorly sealed chamber wastes the nitrogen you buy to keep oxygen down. Both are running costs that never appear on a quotation and always appear on a monthly statement.

Conveyor mechanics fail under heat, not under load

A rail that is stiff at room temperature can deform at 350 °C. A chain that tracks perfectly cold can jump a pin plate hot. That is board jamming, and it is unplanned downtime on the machine that sits in the middle of your line.

02 — The profile

Four phases, and the reason each one exists

A reflow profile is not a temperature ramp. It is four separate jobs performed in sequence on the same board, and the oven either does all four or it does none of them well. The figures below are the IPC profile printed in the machine's own operation manual.

Phase 1 - Preheat

Ramp at 3 °C/s or less up to 120-150 °C. The board and the paste reach a thermal equilibrium before the flux boils off, so the ramp never shocks a sensitive package.

Phase 2 - Dry

A long, slow plateau around 150 °C, deliberately below the 183 °C melting point. Flux activates and the volatiles leave while the paste is still solid, which is what stops a solder ball from forming mid-flight.

Phase 3 - Reflow

Above 183 °C the alloy liquefies. The profile holds 210-230 °C for about 30 seconds so every joint wets fully, then stops before the board is cooked.

Phase 4 - Cool

Rapid cooling down through 150 °C solidifies the joint with a fine grain. Cooling too slowly is what grows the brittle intermetallic layer.

Zone roles, as the manual assigns them

Six upper and six lower zones are controlled independently. The manual maps the first eight channels like this, and is explicit that this is a starting point rather than a recipe: the right numbers depend on the board, the paste and the volume.

Zone 1Upper preheating zone
Zone 2First upper dry zone
Zone 3Second upper dry zone
Zone 4Upper reflow zone
Zone 5Lower preheating zone
Zone 6First lower dry zone
Zone 7Second lower dry zone
Zone 8Lower reflow zone

A real setpoint set

Read off the machine's own control screen in the manual. Ten channels shown, upper and lower, with the peak at 260 °C and a falling last zone.

Z1160 Z2170 Z3180 Z4180 Z5190 Z6190 Z7200 Z8235 Z9260 Z10230
Conveyor speed-5% to -10% · Roughly +30 F at the peak. The manual's worked example takes 500 mm/min down to about 460 mm/min.
Zone setpoint±5 °C per step · Move one zone at a time and re-profile. Never stack two changes into one run.
Fine trim1-5% of belt speed · For the last few degrees, after the coarse speed and setpoint work is done.
Air circulationInverter Hz per fan · Fan inverters are set per zone group; the manual ships them at 30-45 Hz.

Line A - solder paste

Room temperature to 120-150 °C inside about 60 seconds, then 90-150 seconds held near 150 °C, then 30 seconds from 183 °C up to 210-230 °C. This is the profile most boards run on.

Line B - fine pitch and 01005

Slows the rise through the preheat zone so the flux softens later. On a fine-pitch part the failure mode is not the joint, it is the tiny powder particles sintering into a ball before the paste has wetted.

Line C - adhesive cure

A flat 150 °C hold for 3 to 5 minutes. Used when the board goes through a chip shooter with adhesive rather than paste, before wave soldering.

03 — The machine

Hot air that reaches into the shadows

The heating plate is a high-nickel element inside a metal tube packed with calcium silicate. It stores heat and releases it as a laminar curtain of hot air through perforations at a 25 mm pitch — an inner 6 mm hole and an outer 8 mm hole in every position. Laminar flow reaches under a shielded package, which radiant heating cannot do.

Laminar convection, not radiation

Air from the plate reaches the PCB, the components and the paste directly. It heats the solder under a shaded body, transfers to the pad and the paste at the same rate, and keeps two identical components at the same temperature regardless of where they sit on the board.

Independent upper and lower control

Top and bottom heaters are controlled separately. If a package is heat-sensitive the underside can carry the preheat, which is what keeps a large board flat. Roughly half the preheat energy can go into the bottom zones for exactly that reason.

Mechanics that hold their shape at 350°C

A reinforced main hanging bracket, transport rails that have been through a hardening process, and a single pin-plate chain. The point of all three is the same: no rail deformation and no board jamming while the tunnel is hot.

Cooling that pays for itself

Exhaust is captured from the cooling zone, filtered, and returned to the chamber. That cuts the thermal loss and reclaims the flux at the same time, which is why the manual lists a lower cleaning burden than a straight-through exhaust.

Why mesh and not a pin-chain rail

A mesh belt supports a board across its whole underside. That matters when the board is thin, when it is large, and when the bottom zones are doing half the heating work. The trade is that the mesh is a consumable: it stretches, it picks up flux, and it eventually needs replacing. The specification for the belt as built is on the left, and a spare rolls as a single part.

04 — Control

What the operator can see, and what the controller does without being asked

The control station is an industrial PC running PID closed-loop control against high-power SSR drivers, with a PLC and modular circuit behind it for the logic. The interesting part is not the loop itself, it is the audit trail: every zone event is timestamped against an operator name.

Setpoint and process value per zone

Every zone shows its setpoint against its measured value, top and bottom, with a bar for each. The manual's own screen shows a ten-channel layout.

Temperature profile test

Five thermocouple channels, TL1 to TL5, plotted against a ten-minute window with a 160-220 °C delta band. Export to PDF or PNG, or print it for the traveller.

Recipe store and recall

Named recipes with a date stamp. Load a saved parameter set instead of re-keying ten zones.

Alarm and event log

Every zone event, heat start and stop, and language change is timestamped with the operator name. Query by date and export.

Per-zone port debug

Each zone's heater and alarm lamp can be switched individually from the maintenance screen, which is what makes a single failed SSR findable without pulling the tunnel apart.

Auto cutoff

The controller scans every zone once per second and cuts heater power and raises an abnormal alarm if a zone leaves its band.

06 — Options and the nitrogen question

Nitrogen is a running cost, so treat it like one

A sealed chamber that holds a low oxygen level buys you better wetting on a lead-free profile. It also buys a gas bill, every hour, for the life of the machine. The figures below are what the brochure claims; ask for a measured curve on your own board before you budget for them.

Nitrogen atmosphere

The chamber is sealed against gas loss, with an integrated filter that reclaims flux and returns filtered air to the tunnel. Quoted floor is 150 ppm; consumption is 20-22 m3/h in the 300-800 ppm oxygen band.

Dual rail conveyor

Two boards in parallel through the same footprint. The rails are hardened and the chain uses a single pin-plate design, which is what keeps two lanes tracking together at 350 °C.

R to L direction

Standard is left to right. Right to left is available when the line layout demands it.

10-channel HMI

The control software is a shared series platform. It displays more channels than the base machine populates, which is why the screen can look wider than the specification.

07 — Installation

What the site has to provide before the oven arrives

Ambient temperature

5 to 40 °C, whether or not the oven is running.

Relative humidity

20 to 95 percent.

Transport and storage

-25 to 55 °C. Up to 65 °C for less than 24 hours.

Power supply

5-wire 3-phase 380 V, 16 mm2 conductors recommended.

Grounding

Reliable ground, wired by a qualified electrician. 3-phase 5-wire is preferred over 4-wire.

Levelling

Level the machine on its foot cups with an alcohol level until the conveyor chain tracks horizontally.

Air supply

If the line uses pneumatics downstream, allow for 0.5 MPa or better at the drop.

Placement

Clean environment, away from electromagnetic interference. Never face the inlet or the outlet into a fan or an open window.

Pre-start checklist

Twelve checks the manual puts in front of every shift. They take a few minutes and they cover every fault in the fault table below.

  1. Supply is 3-phase 5-wire 380 V plus neutral and ground.
  2. Main circuit conductors in the electrical box are tight.
  3. The machine ground is continuous.
  4. No foreign object inside the electrical box.
  5. Nothing is jamming the mesh belt.
  6. Transmission bearings are lubricated.
  7. High-temperature terminals are not loose or burnt.
  8. The control card is seated.
  9. The drive chain carries high-temperature lubricant.
  10. The exhaust pipe is clear.
  11. The air circulation motor turns freely.
  12. The inverter extension cable is not loose.

09 — What the sources disagree about

Six conflicts, printed side by side

These pages are assembled from a specification sheet, an operation manual and two product brochures. They do not agree everywhere. Rather than pick the flattering number or average the two, we print what each source says, name the source, and say what we would do about it.

Warm-up power

Source A24 kW
Source B12 kW

The spec sheet and the S-6600-PC column of the configuration matrix both say 24 kW. The operation manual's heater table says 12 kW. That table is a series template whose row was never filled in for this model - it lists a 16-zone row under the same heading - so 24 kW is the figure to quote and the manual's 12 kW is flagged.

What we do Quote 24 kW. Confirm against the nameplate before ordering.

Heating zone channels

Source ATop 6 / Bottom 6
Source BZ1 to Z10 on screen

The spec sheet, the brochure and the configuration matrix all say 6 upper and 6 lower. The control screen reproduced in the manual displays channels Z1 to Z10 per side, and its own log records an alarm on the seventh upper zone. The HMI appears to be a shared 10-channel template across the series.

What we do 12 zones is the documented figure. The screen layout is not a zone count.

Drive chain lubrication

Source AEvery 7 days
Source BEvery two months

Both figures are in the same operation manual, four pages apart: section 1.3 says high temperature grease every 7 days, section 2.9 says molybdenum disulphide every two months. They describe different lubricants on the same chain.

What we do Weekly for the chain, two-monthly for the roller and tension rail. Confirm with service.

Warm-up time

Source AAbout 20 minutes
Source B20 to 30 minutes

The spec sheet says about 20 minutes; the manual says 20 to 30 minutes for an annealing furnace. Both are consistent with a cold start at different ambient temperatures.

What we do Plan 20 minutes from warm. 30 in a cold workshop.

Cooling

Source A2 cooling zones
Source B1 cooling fan

The S-6600-PC spec sheet lists 2 cooling zones. The base S-6600 brochure lists 1 cooling fan. These are different machines in the same series, not two readings of one machine.

What we do 2 zones for the PC model. Confirm the cooling arrangement on the order.

Nitrogen performance

Source ALowest 150 ppm
Source B300-800 ppm operating

The brochure quotes a lowest achievable concentration of 150 ppm and, two lines later, a consumption of 20-22 m3/h at 300-800 ppm of oxygen. Read together the 150 ppm is the floor the sealed chamber can hold and 300-800 ppm is the band it runs in.

What we do Ask for a measured O2 curve on your board before committing to a N2 budget.

13 — Insights

Eight notes from inside a lead-free transition

Article bodies stay in English so the process detail is not altered in translation. Headings and standfirsts are translated with the rest of the page.

Your profile is fine until the board changes

A profile is not a setting, it is a measurement of one board on one day. Here is how to tell when it has stopped describing what is on the belt.

The oven has run the same ten setpoints for two years. Nobody has touched it. Then a customer moves a board from 1.0 mm to 1.6 mm and the same setpoints start producing marginal joints at the connector and a slightly browned package next to it.

Nothing failed. That is the problem. A reflow profile is a description of a thermal outcome, not a property of the machine, and it was only ever valid for the board it was measured on. Thickness, copper area, component mass and paste type all move the curve. The setpoints do not move with them.

The reusable method is to stop treating the profile as a constant and start treating it as a four-number budget. Ramp rate under three degrees per second. A soak band below the melting point. Time above liquidus. Peak. If you can name those four numbers for a board, you can re-derive the setpoints for its successor in an afternoon instead of a week of trial runs.

That is why the profile test function matters more than the setpoint screen. Five thermocouple channels over a ten-minute window, a delta band you define, and an export you can attach to the traveller. The machine in this class does exactly that: it measures the board, rather than asserting a temperature.

The habit worth building is to re-measure on a trigger, not on a calendar. A new board revision, a new paste lot, a new panel array, a replaced heater. Each of those is a reason to run one test plate, and each of them is cheap compared to a batch that has to be reworked.

If you send us a board and the paste you use, we will run the profile and send back the curve with the zone setpoints and the belt speed that produced it. Compare it against your own oven. If the two agree, you have learned something useful about your line for free.

The zones you never look at are doing half the work

Most operators profile from the top because that is where the thermocouples go. The bottom half of the tunnel is where warpage is won or lost.

Watch someone set up a reflow oven and you will see them adjust the upper zones. The lower zones are usually left at whatever the last engineer entered. That is backwards for any board with a large ground plane or a heavy connector on it.

Heat from above has to cross the components to reach the board. Heat from below crosses nothing. When the top does all the work, the paste reaches temperature before the board does, the board bows, and the parts at the edges see a different profile from the parts in the middle. The failure looks like a placement problem and it is a thermal one.

The method is to move roughly half the preheat energy into the bottom zones and use the top only to hold the surface at temperature. Bottom-heavy preheat warms the board through its thickness before the paste is asked to do anything, which flattens the board and flattens the curve at the same time.

Independent upper and lower control is what makes that possible, and it is the reason the zone count matters more than the zone number on the brochure. Twelve zones with six underneath is a different machine from twelve zones with all the heat on top. The control screen shows setpoint against measured value for every channel, top and bottom, so you can see which half is carrying the load.

The reason to come back to this is that the right split is not a constant either. A thin flex board wants almost nothing underneath. A 2.4 mm backplane wants a lot. Once you have found the split for one board family, write it into the recipe name and it becomes the starting point for the next one.

Take your worst-warping board and run it with the bottom zones raised by fifteen degrees and the top zones lowered by the same amount. Keep the peak where it is. Measure the flatness before and after. That single experiment usually settles the argument.

Nitrogen is not a feature, it is a monthly bill

A sealed chamber buys better wetting and costs money every hour it is closed. Do the arithmetic before you accept the option.

Nitrogen gets sold as a quality feature. It is better understood as a utility, like compressed air or electricity, with one difference: nobody asks what it costs per board before they tick the box.

The cost is continuous and it is invisible. A chamber that is not well sealed leaks gas you paid for. A chamber that is well sealed still consumes gas at a rate set by its oxygen target, and that rate is quoted at a specific operating band. A figure like twenty to twenty-two cubic metres an hour means very little until you multiply it by your gas price and your running hours.

The method is to treat the oxygen level as a process variable with a cost curve. Find the highest oxygen concentration at which your worst board still wets acceptably, and run there. Every ten parts per million you give back is gas you stop buying, and on a lead-free profile the difference between two hundred and eight hundred parts per million is often invisible in the joint.

This is where the reclaim loop earns its place. Exhaust captured from the cooling zone, filtered and returned to the chamber, cuts both the gas consumption and the thermal loss. The same filter is doing flux reclamation, so the maintenance burden comes down as well. One mechanism, three effects.

Come back to this whenever your production mix changes. A board with a large exposed pad area tolerates a much higher oxygen level than a fine-pitch part with a low paste volume. If you are running both on one line, the nitrogen setting should change between them, and most lines never do.

Before you commit to a gas budget, ask for a measured oxygen curve on your own board rather than a chamber specification. If a supplier cannot produce that curve, that tells you something useful too.

Thirty seconds at 220 is not the same as sixty at 200

Time above liquidus is the number that decides whether a joint is reliable. Peak temperature is the number people argue about.

Two profiles with the same peak can produce joints with completely different fatigue life. The peak is what the operator watches. The time above liquidus is what the joint remembers.

Below the melting point nothing metallurgically interesting happens. Above it, the alloy wets the pad, the intermetallic layer grows, and the joint becomes what it will be for the rest of its life. Too little time and the wetting is incomplete. Too much and the intermetallic layer grows thick and brittle. Both failures pass a visual inspection.

The method is to fix the time above liquidus first and let the peak follow. For most lead-free assemblies that means roughly thirty seconds above the alloy's melting point, with the peak arriving somewhere between two hundred and ten and two hundred and thirty degrees. Once the dwell is right, the peak becomes a fine adjustment rather than the main event.

The manual's own worked profile makes this concrete. It ramps to a hundred and twenty to a hundred and fifty degrees inside a minute, holds near a hundred and fifty for a minute and a half to two and a half minutes, and then spends thirty seconds climbing from a hundred and eighty-three to the peak. The dry phase is deliberately long and deliberately below the melting point of the tin-lead alloy, at a hundred and eighty-three degrees, which is the reference the whole curve is measured against.

The reason this rewards a second visit is that dwell time is the variable most sensitive to board change. Add copper to a layer and the dwell shortens without anything on the setpoint screen moving. If you have a number for time above liquidus, you have a way to notice.

Next time you profile a board, print the curve and write the time above liquidus on it by hand. Keep it with the board. When the board changes, you have a baseline to compare against rather than a memory.

The belt speed number that quietly decides your yield

Speed is the only control that changes every zone at once. That makes it the most powerful and the most misused setting on the machine.

Ask an operator what the belt speed is and you will usually get a number. Ask why it is that number and you will usually get a shrug. It is the setting that everyone touches and nobody owns.

Speed sets the dwell time in every zone simultaneously. Lower it and the board gets hotter everywhere at once. Raise it and the whole curve compresses. That is why it is the fastest way to fix a profile and the fastest way to break one, and why adjusting speed and temperature together is how a process becomes unrepeatable.

The method is to change one thing per run. If the board is under-reflowed, take the speed down by five to ten percent and re-profile. The manual's own rule of thumb is that a ten percent reduction in belt speed is worth about thirty degrees Fahrenheit at the peak, which is a large enough move to see immediately. If that is not enough, change a zone setpoint by five degrees and re-profile again.

Speed is also the number that connects the oven to the rest of the line. A tunnel that runs at two thousand millimetres a minute on a two hundred and fifty millimetre board with a fifty millimetre gap is passing roughly eight boards a minute. If the printer upstream cannot feed that, the extra speed is not throughput, it is idle time.

This is worth revisiting every time the panel array changes. Board length along the flow is the number people forget, and it changes the cycle time linearly. Two boards of different length at the same speed produce different throughput, and the same profile may no longer be valid for the longer one.

Measure your board length, measure your gap, and put both into the calculator on this page along with your conveyor speed. If the boards-per-hour figure it returns is not the figure your production plan assumes, you have found a gap between the plan and the machine.

Cold joints on one component, damage on the next

The same profile can underheat a connector and overheat the package beside it. Laminar hot air is the reason, and the fix is geometric rather than thermal.

A board comes off the line with a cold joint on a through-hole connector and a browned plastic body on the fine-pitch part eight millimetres away. Both parts saw the same profile. Only one of them saw the same temperature.

The cause is thermal mass and shadowing. A heavy connector acts as a heat sink and pulls energy out of the joint while the surrounding air is already at setpoint. A package with a low mass and a dark body absorbs the same energy and gets hotter. Radiant heating makes this worse, because it heats surfaces rather than air and it cannot reach under a body at all.

The method is to heat with a moving fluid rather than with radiation, and to give the fluid a path under the obstruction. Laminar hot air blown down through a perforated plate reaches under a shielded package and transfers to the pad and the paste at the same rate as it transfers to the open board beside them. The plate in this class of machine carries an inner six millimetre and an outer eight millimetre hole at a twenty-five millimetre pitch, which is what produces a laminar curtain rather than a turbulent blast.

The other half of the fix is bottom-side heat. If the heavy part is the problem, warming the board from underneath brings its mass up to temperature without adding energy to the sensitive package on top. That is the practical reason independent upper and lower zone control exists.

The reason to come back is that the geometry changes with every new board. A connector that was fine on the last design can shadow a different neighbour on this one. The question to ask at every design review is not what temperature the profile reaches but which components are being shielded from the airflow.

Pick the worst mixed-mass board you have, put thermocouples on both the heavy and the light part, and run it. The two curves will tell you more about your oven than a month of setpoint adjustments.

What your alarm log knows that you do not

A reflow oven writes down every zone event with a timestamp and an operator name. Almost nobody reads it until something fails.

Somewhere in the control software there is a list of every temperature excursion, every heat start, every time the language was changed, each one stamped with a time and the name of whoever was logged in. It is the most useful document on the machine and it is almost never opened.

That log is where intermittent faults live. A zone that briefly leaves its band once a shift will not show up on a spot check of the setpoint screen, and it will not stop the line. It will produce a slightly different joint every few hundred boards, and the quality team will spend a month blaming the paste.

The method is to treat the log as a leading indicator rather than a record. Query it by date at the end of each week and look for the same zone appearing twice. One excursion is noise. The same channel twice in a week is a thermocouple drifting or a solid state relay beginning to fail, and both are cheap to replace before they cost a batch.

This only works if the machine writes the log without being asked. The controller in this class scans every zone once per second and cuts heater power and raises an abnormal alarm if a channel leaves its band, so the record is generated by the safety function rather than by an operator remembering to press something. The log is queryable by date range and exportable.

There is a second use for the same file. When a customer disputes a batch, a timestamped log with zone values is the difference between a conversation about evidence and a conversation about opinions. Machines that keep one are easier to defend.

Open the log on your own oven this week and look for the last thirty days. Count how many times the same zone appears. If the answer is more than twice, you already have your next maintenance task.

Twelve zones is a statement about the bottom half

Zone count is usually sold as a throughput number. It is really a statement about how independently the top and bottom of the board can be heated.

Brochures present zone count as if more zones meant a faster oven. Speed comes from belt length and conveyor rate. What zone count actually buys is resolution: how finely the profile can be shaped, and how separately the two faces of the board can be treated.

That distinction matters most at the transition points. A profile has three places where the slope has to change sharply: the end of the ramp, the start of reflow, and the beginning of the cool. A machine with few zones has to make those transitions inside one long zone, which means the board either soaks too long or ramps too fast. More zones let each transition happen in its own chamber.

The method is to count zones in pairs. Six upper and six lower is twelve channels, but it is six decisions, because each pair is one position along the tunnel. Ask what each pair is for before you ask how many there are. In this class of machine the manual assigns them explicitly: preheat, two dry stages and a reflow stage on each side.

The lower half is the part worth interrogating. If a machine's bottom zones are mirror images of the top zones with no independent control, the second half of the zone count is decoration. The control screen will tell you: if every lower channel tracks its upper partner exactly, they are not independent.

The reason to come back is that zone assignment changes with the product. A board that needs a long dry phase wants the middle pairs doing the work. A board with a heavy connector wants the lower preheat pair carrying more. The recipe store exists so that those assignments can be recalled by name instead of re-derived.

Before your next oven purchase, ask the supplier to show you the zone assignment for a board like yours and to explain why the lower zones are set where they are. A supplier who can answer that is selling a process. One who cannot is selling a box.

15 — Questions we get asked

Straight answers, including the awkward ones

What is the difference between the S-6600 and the S-6600-PC?

Heating length, board width, conveyor speed and control interface. The base S-6600 has 1800 mm of heating, a 300 mm maximum board and a 0-1500 mm/min conveyor driven by an instrument controller. The S-6600-PC extends that to 2300 mm, 350 mm and 0-2000 mm/min, and puts an industrial PC in front of it. The zone count is 6 upper and 6 lower on both.

How many heating zones does the S-6600-PC actually have?

Twelve: six upper and six lower. That is what the specification sheet, the brochure and the configuration matrix all say. The control screen shown in the operation manual displays ten channels per side because the HMI is a shared series platform, and the manual's own zone notes reference a tenth zone. We flag the difference rather than pick one.

Is 24 kW or 12 kW the right warm-up power?

24 kW is the figure we quote, from the specification sheet and the configuration matrix. The operation manual's heater table says 12 kW, but that table is a series template whose row was never filled in for this model. Ask us for the nameplate photograph on your build.

Can it run nitrogen?

Yes, the chamber is sealed against gas loss and includes a flux-reclaiming filter that returns filtered air to the tunnel. The quoted floor is 150 ppm and consumption is 20-22 m3/h in the 300-800 ppm oxygen band. Because nitrogen is a running cost, ask for a measured O2 curve on your own board before you commit to a budget.

What board size and throughput should I expect?

Up to 350 mm wide on the PC model, at conveyor speeds to 2000 mm/min. Throughput is not a fixed number: it follows from your board length, your panel gap and the dwell your paste needs. The calculator on this page takes those three and gives you boards per hour, so you can check the number against your own line.

How long does it take to warm up, and what does it draw when it is running?

About 20 minutes to reach a stable profile, 20 to 30 minutes from a cold workshop. Warm-up power is 24 kW; once the tunnel is at temperature the operating draw is 3-5 kW, because the zones are only replacing losses at that point.

What maintenance does it need?

Seven intervals are documented: drive chain weekly, bearings monthly, roller and tension rail every two months, conveyor motor at least twice a week, fans weekly, case and exhaust daily, and a ground continuity check before every start. The weekly and two-monthly chain figures come from two different sections of the manual and describe different lubricants, so we print both.

What happens if a zone overheats?

The controller scans every zone once per second. If a zone leaves its band it cuts heater power and raises an abnormal temperature alarm, and the event is written to the timestamped log. Each zone's heater and alarm lamp can also be switched individually from the port debug screen, so a failed SSR is findable without dismantling the tunnel.
